paragraphs.heading: A tree made of stone
paragraphs.text: Petrified wood is a kind of fossil wood, the remains of plants that grew on land. The name comes from the Ancient Greek word petra, meaning rock or stone, and it fits: the tree has been replaced by stone through mineralization, often by permineralization and replacement. Minerals copy the stuff the cell walls were made of, and the mineral is usually silica, appearing as opal, chalcedony or quartz. Most plant fossils are flat impressions or compressions, but petrified wood keeps the full three-dimensional shape of the original wood.

paragraphs.heading: Shutting out the air
paragraphs.text: The change happens underground, after wood is buried in water or volcanic ash. Water cuts down the oxygen supply, which holds back the bacteria and fungi that would otherwise break the wood down. Keeping oxygen out is the single most important factor, because the organisms that decompose lignin need oxygen to live. Burial is not always kind, though: wood buried in alkaline surroundings is quickly destroyed by chemical reactions.

paragraphs.heading: What wood is made of
paragraphs.text: Wood is mostly holocellulose, which means cellulose plus hemicellulose, together with lignin; these make up 95% of dry wood. Almost half is cellulose, which gives wood much of its strength. Microbes normally break dead wood down fast, starting with the holocellulose, while lignin repels water and rots much more slowly. Fossil wood older than the Eocene, about 56 million years or more, has lost nearly all its holocellulose and keeps only lignin.

paragraphs.heading: From wood to rock
paragraphs.text: Water loaded with minerals flows through the buried sediment. In permineralization, minerals settle out of that water and fill the insides of cells and other empty spaces. In replacement, the cell walls act as a mold: silica bonds to the cellulose in the walls through hydrogen bonding, then more silica takes the cellulose's place as it decays. This is why cell walls are often kept in great detail. In the end only about 10% of the original organic material is left.

paragraphs.heading: The minerals involved
paragraphs.text: Around 40 minerals have been found in petrified wood, but silica minerals matter far more than the rest. Calcite and pyrite show up much less often, and the others are rare. Scientists are still working out what form the silica takes first. Some evidence points to opal that slowly turns into quartz over long spans of time, while other evidence suggests silica goes straight in as quartz.

paragraphs.heading: Forests that outlast erosion
paragraphs.text: Petrified wood usually comes from trees buried in the fine sediments of deltas and floodplains or in volcanic lahars and ash beds, and a forest preserved this way is called a petrified forest. Later, erosion strips away the surrounding sediment and brings the wood to the surface. Unmineralized fossil wood falls apart quickly once exposed, but petrified wood is very tough. Things can also move fast: in hot springs rich in silica, wood can turn to silica within hundreds of years. Such hot spring wood is a small part of the record, but it sometimes keeps delicate plant parts in superb detail.
